justification: The known bug is that context.ts passes every pipe in the component's scope, not just the pipes the template uses, into the now-stricter canReferenceType check. That forces inlining unnecessarily. Finding [0] does not raise this. It asks whether `canReferenceType` exists at all, and whether its semantics match the old export check. It never mentions that `pipes` covers all in-scope pipes rather than only the used ones.
ground_truth: `requiresInlineTypeCheckBlock` now requires an inline type-check block whenever any pipe in its `usedPipes` argument cannot be referenced from the TCB environment (`env.canReferenceType`, stricter than the previous "is exported" check). But the caller in context.ts passes `pipes`, the map of all pipes in the component's scope, not just those used in the template. Components that merely have an unreferenceable pipe in scope are now forced to inline, which errors where inlining is unsupported (e.g. the language service reports spurious errors). Fixed by passing only the pipes the template actually uses.

findings.description: The change calls `env.canReferenceType(ref)` on `ReferenceEmitEnvironment`, but the diff does not add that method or touch the environment class. If it is not already defined, this will not compile. The replacement `canReferenceType` check must also match the old `checkIfClassIsExported` semantics for exported classes, including ones exported via `export {}` and via aliases. Otherwise some non-exported classes may be treated as referenceable and get a non-inline TCB, or the reverse.

justification: Finding 0 pins the defect to the skip condition: `part.match(_placeholderRe)` also fires on SafeSelector's placeholders for attribute selectors such as `[attr]`. It gives `[x]>b` as an example where the child combinator is swallowed because the next character is hex. That is the same mechanism as the `:host[foo]>div` case in the known bug, and its suggested fix of checking only for escape placeholders lines up with the actual fix.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The new skip condition is too broad. `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true when any placeholder appears anywhere in the part, and `selector[res.index + 1]` is tested against hex characters for every separator type. SafeSelector also uses placeholders for attribute selectors such as `[attr]`, for `:nth-*` expressions, and for escaped selectors. So `input[type=text] a {}`, `.foo[bar] div {}`, `[x]>b` and `.one\:two div` are all wrongly treated as 'not a separator' when the next token starts with a-f or a digit. The descendant or child combinator is then swallowed and the following compound selector is never scoped. This regresses ordinary selectors, because those parts would no longer get the `[contenta]` attribute. The check should apply only when the separator is a space and the part ends with an escape placeholder.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty guard. It says `part.match(_placeholderRe)` "is true for any placeholder", including the attribute-selector placeholders that SafeSelector creates. As a result, a separator followed by a hex character is wrongly skipped and the selector is scoped incorrectly. Its examples use a space combinator rather than `>`, but the mechanism is the same. Its suggested fix, distinguishing escape placeholders from other placeholders, also matches the real fix.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The guard `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true for any placeholder, not only one created for an escaped hex sequence. SafeSelector also replaces attribute selectors such as `[type=text]` and `:nth-*(...)` arguments with `__ph-N__`. A descendant combinator after one of those, followed by an element name that starts with a hex character, is therefore wrongly treated as an escape-terminating space. Examples are `[x] div`, `a[href] em` and `input[type=text] button`. The separator is skipped and the parts are not scoped separately, so the second compound selector loses its `[contenta]` attribute. This regresses component style encapsulation for common selectors. The check should confirm that the placeholder is an escape (backslash plus hex digits) at the end of `part`.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty condition: it says "it fires whenever the pending `part` contains any `__ph-N__` placeholder and the character after the separator is a hex digit" and notes that "placeholders are also used for attribute selectors (`[attr]`)". It then shows the same consequence, separators being swallowed and the preceding part going unscoped, including for `>` separators. This is the same mechanism as the known bug's `:host[foo]>div` case.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The new skip condition is far too broad. It fires whenever the pending `part` contains any `__ph-N__` placeholder and the character after the separator is a hex digit. It does not check that the placeholder is an escape sequence, that the separator is a space, or that the placeholder ends the part. Placeholders are also used for attribute selectors (`[attr]`) and `:nth-*(...)` expressions. So `[type=text] button {}`, `div[foo] a {}`, `.x:nth-child(2n+1) b {}` and `.a\:b .c {}` are all treated as one compound selector. The descendant combinator is swallowed and the preceding part is never scoped. This is a regression: `[type=text] button` now becomes `[type=text] button[contenta]` instead of `[type=text][contenta] button[contenta]`, breaking style encapsulation. The check also ignores the separator type, so `.a\:b>a`, `.a\:b+b` and `.a\:b~c` (with `>`, `+`, `~` as the separator) are skipped as well.

justification: Finding 0 identifies exactly the removed guards in test_hooks.ts. It explains that `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally and that this throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined` when no test framework defines them. That is the same defect and mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: While replacing `global` with `globalThis`, the PR removed the guards around the Jasmine/Jest hooks in `@angular/core/testing` test_hooks.ts: `if (_global.beforeEach) {...}` became an unconditional `beforeEach(...)` / `afterEach(...)`. When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework defines these globals (for example when it ends up in a server bundle, or in a non-Jasmine/Mocha runner), module evaluation throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code tolerated this case.

justification: Finding 0 pinpoints the removed `if (_global.beforeEach)`/`afterEach` guards in test_hooks.ts, noting that the hooks are now called unconditionally at module load. It also identifies that evaluating the module outside a test framework throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. This is exactly the known bug.

When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework globals exist, for example when the file ends up in a server bundle or a non-Jasmine/Mocha/Jest runner, evaluating the module throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. This is a regression from the previously safe behavior.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says the removed `if (_global.beforeEach)` guards mean `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` now run unconditionally at module load. It also says this throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined` when the module is loaded outside a test framework. That is the known bug's faulty code and failure mechanism.

When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The old `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework has defined these globals (e.g. server bundles, a non-Jasmine/Mocha runner, or a tool that loads the module), it throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code tolerated this case. This is a behavior regression, not a pure refactor.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug exactly. It states that `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never updated in `collectDeferredSymbols`, so the per-block deps fns emit `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`. It also proposes the same fix as the known bug. Finding 1 describes a different issue: mixed default and named imports misclassified by the `isDefaultImport` helper.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: In `collectDeferredSymbols`, `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never updated. It is initialised to `false` in the dependency collection and the loop only sets `isDeferrable` and `importPath`. The `isDefaultImport` value goes only into the `deferrableTypes` map. The compiler paths that read `deferredDep.isDefaultImport` or `dep.isDefaultImport` (`template.ts`, `create_defer_deps_fns.ts`) therefore always emit `m => m.CmpA`. For a default-imported component that resolves to `undefined` at runtime, which breaks the lazy-loaded dependency function. The new test expecting `m => m.default` in `TestCmp_Defer_1_DepsFn` would fail. The fix is to set `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)`.

`isDefaultImport` treats an import as default only when there are no named bindings. For `import Default, {Other} from './x'`, `namedBindings` is defined, so it returns false. A deferred default-imported symbol then gets `m.Symbol` instead of `m.default`. The check is per declaration, not per identifier.

justification: The known bug is that `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never set in `collectDeferredSymbols`, so per-block deps keep `false` even for simple default imports. Finding [0] criticizes the `isDefaultImport()` heuristic, saying it mishandles mixed imports or `{default as X}`. That is a different defect, and it would not lead a maintainer to the missing assignment on the per-block dependency objects.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: isDefaultImport() returns true only when the import has no namedBindings. For a mixed import such as `import CmpA, {Other} from './cmp-a'`, or `import {default as CmpA} from './cmp-a'`, namedBindings is defined, so a default-bound symbol is reported as non-default. The generated dynamic import then uses `m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. Conversely, with `import Default, {Named}`, the check does not look at which binding the symbol actually uses.

justification: The known bug is that `collectDeferredSymbols` never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects, so they stay `false`. As a result, the per-block loader emits `m.Name` even for a plain default import. Finding [0] describes a different mechanism: `isDefaultImport()` misclassifying combined imports like `import CmpA, {Other}` because of how it checks named bindings. It does not identify the missing assignment on `deferBlockDep`, so it does not match.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: isDefaultImport() returns false whenever the import has named bindings. For a combined import such as `import CmpA, {Other} from './cmp-a'`, where CmpA is the default import and is used in a @defer block or deferredImports, the generated loader becomes `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`. At runtime that resolves to undefined and the deferred dependency fails to load.

justification: The known bug is that `copyEventListenerOptions` uses object spread, which drops getter, prototype and non-enumerable option properties (`capture`, `once`, `passive`). Finding [0] instead raises re-entrancy on the shared `taskData` affecting the `once` restore ("`taskData.options` can be overwritten... nested `addEventListener`"). That is a different mechanism, and it does not concern the spread losing properties.
ground_truth: To avoid mutating readonly/frozen listener options, the PR copies them with `{...options}` in `copyEventListenerOptions` before passing them to the native `addEventListener` (special-casing only `signal`). Object spread copies only own enumerable data properties, while the native call reads each option via [[Get]]. Options supplied as getters, on the prototype, or as non-enumerable properties are silently dropped: `capture: true` becomes bubbling, `once: true` fires repeatedly, and the MDN `passive` feature-detection getter is never invoked. Fixed by also reading `capture`, `once`, `passive` and `signal` from the source object when the spread did not copy them.

findings.description: The post-schedule restore of `once` now uses `taskData.options.once = true`. `taskData` is a shared global object, so `taskData.options` can be overwritten if `scheduleEventTask` or a zone hook (such as `onScheduleTask`) triggers a nested `addEventListener`. In that case the `once` flag would be set on the wrong options object, or the local `options` would never get `once` restored. The previous code used the local `options` reference, which is safe against this.

justification: Neither finding identifies the actual defect. The real bug is that relative links resolve against the ActivatedRoute, so their href changes after any navigation; gating the NavigationEnd subscription on preserveFragment or queryParamsHandling leaves those hrefs stale. Finding 0 is about the inverted `isAnchorElement` branch and its effect on tabindex and accessibility, which is a different issue. Finding 1 says the default-handling clause is inverted ("skips the subscription when the default IS 'merge' or 'preserve'"). The ground truth explicitly names this as a different defect, because flipping that clause would remove subscriptions in other cases rather than always subscribing. Neither finding notes that relative links depend on route changes regardless of query or fragment handling.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The condition is inverted. `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary() } else { setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0') }` now sets tabindex=0 on real anchor and area elements and skips it for non-anchor hosts such as div or button. Non-anchor routerLink elements lose keyboard focusability, which is an accessibility regression. The subscribe call is also a no-op there, because it returns early for non-anchors.

The subscription condition for the case with no `queryParamsHandling` on the link is inverted. It subscribes when the router's default handling is NOT merge/preserve, and skips the subscription when the default IS 'merge' or 'preserve'. With `defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge'` or `'preserve'` and no per-link setting, the href depends on current router state but never updates on NavigationEnd. The href goes stale after query params change.

justification: Finding [0] flags the inverted `if (!this.isAnchorElement)` check in the constructor, which wrongly sets tabindex on anchors and defers the subscription to ngOnChanges. The known bug is different: `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` only subscribes when the link depends on router state (preserveFragment, merge/preserve). That premise is wrong, because relative links also need their href recomputed after any navigation. The finding never questions that gating logic or mentions stale relative-link hrefs. It even implies subscriptions still happen after ngOnChanges, so it would not lead a maintainer to the real defect.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The condition in the constructor is inverted. `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { this.subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary(); } else { this.setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0'); }`. For non-anchor hosts the helper returns immediately, so the call does nothing. For anchor hosts (`<a>`, `<area>`, compatible custom elements) the else branch runs and sets `tabindex="0"` on a natively focusable element, which is a behavior regression. Anchors also skip the NavigationEnd subscription in the constructor, so href is only subscribed after the first ngOnChanges. Non-anchor elements still get the tabindex. The condition should be `if (this.isAnchorElement)`.

justification: Finding 0 is the case the ground truth explicitly excludes. It says the default-handling clause is inverted and that the fix is to subscribe only when the default depends on router state ("It should be `!this.queryParamsHandling && dependsOnRouterState(default)`"). That would subscribe in fewer cases and drop subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix. It never mentions that relative links depend on the ActivatedRoute changing. Finding 1 is about the swapped constructor branches and the lost tabindex, which is a different issue. It also accepts that anchors subscribe via ngOnChanges and does not identify that the subscription condition itself is wrong.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The condition for subscribing to NavigationEnd is inverted. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes when the default does NOT depend on router state, and skips it when the router-wide `defaultQueryParamsHandling` is 'merge' or 'preserve'. In that case a link with no per-link handling has an href that depends on the current query params, but it never updates after navigation, so the href goes stale. It also creates needless subscriptions for plain links. It should be `!this.queryParamsHandling && dependsOnRouterState(default)`.

The constructor branches are swapped. `if (!this.isAnchorElement) subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary() else setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` calls the subscribe helper only for non-anchors, where it returns immediately. It calls the tabindex setter only for anchors, where it also returns immediately. The original constructor-time `tabindex=0` for non-anchor hosts is lost, and no subscription is created in the constructor for anchors. Anchors now depend entirely on ngOnChanges for the subscription.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same mechanism: `first()` throws EmptyError when the source completes without emitting, where `toPromise()` resolved undefined. It explicitly extends this to "the other call sites in `recognize.ts` if a source completes empty". Those call sites are where the known bug lives (matchWithChecks, runCanLoadGuards, loadChildren). The finding leads with the redirectTo example, but it names the same faulty behavior in the same code. That would lead a maintainer to the actual bug.
ground_truth: The PR replaces `.toPromise()` with a custom `firstValueFrom` (built on rxjs `first()`) in route recognition (`matchWithChecks`, `runCanLoadGuards`, `loadChildren`). Unlike `toPromise()`, which resolves `undefined` when an observable completes without emitting, `first()` errors with an EmptyError. Guards or matchers whose observables complete without emitting now throw EmptyError instead of being treated as "no match"; the recognizer's catch only skips NoMatch errors, so navigation fails instead of moving on to the next route. Fixed by also treating EmptyError as a non-match in recognize.ts.

findings.description: The `firstValueFrom` replacement uses `first()`, which errors with EmptyError when the source completes without emitting. The `toPromise()` it replaces resolved with `undefined` in that case. A `redirectTo` function returning an empty observable (for example `EMPTY`) used to resolve to `undefined`. It now rejects the promise with EmptyError, and the navigation fails with an error instead of going through the previous handling. The same applies to the other call sites in `recognize.ts` if a source completes empty.

justification: Finding [0] describes the same defect. It notes that `leavingNodes` is "keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance", and that when "instance A's element is still animating out in parent X and instance B is created in parent Y", A's "leave animation is then cancelled and the element removed." This is the same cross-parent removal mechanism as the known bug. The other findings cover a different heuristic (previousSibling), the queue dequeue removal, and performance concerns, so they do not match.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: The "different DOM parent" condition cancels and force-removes leaving elements that have nothing to do with the new element. leavingNodes is keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance of a component or template. If instance A's element is still animating out in parent X and instance B is created in parent Y, B's insert finds A with a different parent. A's leave animation is then cancelled and the element removed. This breaks legitimate leave animations for reused components, for example the same component rendered in two places.

The previousSibling check is only a heuristic for an @if toggle. When a leaving element is adjacent to a newly inserted element of the same TNode, it is cancelled even though it is a different logical item. An example is an @for list where one item leaves and a new item is inserted immediately after it, or a whole list is replaced. The leaving element's animation is cut short and the element removed early.

The removal of removeAnimationsFromQueue means enter animations still queued for a node are no longer dequeued when that node is removed. If the node is removed before the animation queue flushes, for example on a quick toggle, the stale enter animation functions still run against a detached or leaving element. This can add enter classes or listeners to a node that is leaving, and can interfere with the leave animation.

cancelLeavingNodes is called on every native insert of every node, including text and comment nodes and nodes in apps that use no animations. The rNode is cast to HTMLElement, and the function and the leavingNodes map are now pulled into every bundle (the golden symbols changed in all of them). Because the same function runs for every insert, this adds overhead and a coupling to the animation code on a hot path.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It notes that "`leavingNodes` is keyed by `tNode`, which is shared by every instance" and that the different-parent check cancels leave animations of unrelated instances inserted into different hosts. This is exactly the known bug's mechanism. Finding 1 describes a different concern: removed queued enter animations.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: `leavingNodes` is keyed by `tNode`, which is shared by every instance of a template or component, and `cancelLeavingNodes` now treats any leaving element with a different DOM parent as a duplicate. If instance A is leaving in parent P1 and another instance of the same template is inserted into P2, A's leave animation is cut short. This happens for lists of components or embedded views that each have `animate.leave` and sit in different hosts. `animationend` is dispatched with `cancel: true` and A is removed immediately, which is a regression for unrelated instances. The overlay heuristic is too broad for this.

The code that removed queued enter animations from the animation queue when a node is detached has been deleted, as has `removeAnimationsFromQueue`. If an element is created and then removed before the queue is flushed, its enter animation functions still run against a detached element. This can cause errors or stale animation state on removed nodes. Nothing else cancels those queued functions.

justification: Finding 1 describes the same defect. It says `leavingNodes` is "keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance". As a result, a new insert of another instance in a different parent "cancels and force-removes the first instance's leaving element", which cuts off a legitimate leave animation. That is exactly the cross-parent heuristic bug. Finding 0 is a different mechanism: stale tracking from moves combined with previousSibling. Finding 2 concerns the removed enter-queue cleanup, which is unrelated.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: trackLeavingNodes is called on every Detach of a node whose TNode has a leave animation. That includes plain detaches and moves such as @for reordering or ViewContainerRef.move, where the element is reinserted and no leave animation ever runs. The live element then stays in `leavingNodes` and is never cleared. A later Insert for the same TNode, such as a newly added @for item placed right after it, sees that element as `previousSibling`. `cancelLeavingNodes` then dispatches a cancel event and calls `removeChild` on a live, visible element. The stale entries also keep detached elements alive.

The 'different DOM parent' heuristic is wrong because `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance of a component or template. When one instance's element is animating out in parent X and another instance of the same component inserts its element in a different parent Y, the new insert cancels and force-removes the first instance's leaving element. This cuts off a legitimate leave animation, for example in lists of components that each use @if with animate.leave. The check cannot tell the overlay/portal case from unrelated instances.

The removal of `removeAnimationsFromQueue` means a queued enter animation is no longer dropped when the element is detached before the queue flushes. With rapid toggling, the enter animation can still run on an element that is already leaving. It adds enter classes to it, may register enter listeners, and `cleanupEnterClassData` may interfere with the leave animation. This is a behavioral regression for quick toggles in the same parent.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It states that `position` used to be serialized as '0,1,2' and is now sent as "[0,1,2]". It also notes that the consumers `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` were not updated, so 'view source' and 'select DOM element' break. The backend that parses this serialized id still expects the comma-separated format, so "view source" and "select DOM element" from the component tree break. The fix updates the backend (component-tree.ts) to the new format; the PR changed the wire format without updating its consumer.

findings.description: The serialization format of `position` changed. Previously the array was interpolated into a quoted string, which produced a comma-separated value like '0,1,2'. Now `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]". The diff does not change `findConstructorByPosition` or `findDomElementByPosition`. If those still parse with `split(',').map(Number)`, the first and last elements become NaN, and 'view source' and 'select DOM element' break. The same format change applies to `selectDomElement` at line 26.

findings.description: `position` is an array, and the old template literal turned it into a comma-separated string like `0,1,2`. View Source then resolves the wrong element or fails. The change touches only this file, so the receiver was not updated to match.

findings.description: `position` is an ElementPosition (number[]). It used to be interpolated as `'${position}'`, which produces a comma-joined string like "0,1,2". The receiving `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` helpers most likely parse that format with `split(',').map(parseInt)`. `stringifyAndEscape(position)` now passes the string "[0,1,2]" instead. Splitting it on commas gives "[0" and "2]", and parseInt turns "[0" into NaN, so the lookup fails. 'View source' and 'select DOM element' would then break. Only the sender was changed, and the receivers were not updated to JSON.parse. The fix is to serialize with `JSON.stringify(position.join(','))`, or update the receivers.

`selectDomElement` has the same problem. The position array is now sent as a JSON-array string ("[0,1]") where the receiver expects a comma-separated list of indexes ("0,1"). The first index is parsed as NaN, so the element cannot be found.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says that for legend tags "attrs is no longer copied into a new dict", so the required_css_class block mutates "the caller's own dict". It also notes the 'required' class then accumulates when the dict is reused. This is the same faulty code and failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: Previously `label_tag()` built a fresh dict (`{**(attrs or {}), "for": ...}`) before adding the required CSS class. To omit "for" on <legend> tags, the commit uses `attrs = attrs or {}` and only copies when `tag != "legend"`. For legends (`legend_tag()`) the caller's own dict is kept, and the following `attrs["class"] += " " + required_css_class` mutates it in place. The caller's attrs dict is modified and the class accumulates on repeated rendering. Fixed by always copying attrs first.

findings.description: For `legend` tags, `attrs` is no longer copied into a new dict because the `{**attrs, "for": ...}` step is skipped. The `required_css_class` block that follows then does `attrs["class"] += ...` or `attrs["class"] = ...` on the caller's own dict. When `legend_tag(attrs=...)` is called with a required field and a form that sets `required_css_class`, the caller's dict is mutated. Reusing that dict, for example across several fields, makes the `required` class accumulate. Before this change the dict was always copied when `id_for_label` was set.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It says that for legends "`attrs` is no longer copied" and that the following `attrs["class"] += ...` "mutates the caller's dict", so the class "grow[s] with each call". That is the same faulty code and the same in-place mutation mechanism described in the known bug.
ground_truth: Previously `label_tag()` built a fresh dict (`{**(attrs or {}), "for": ...}`) before adding the required CSS class. To omit "for" on <legend> tags, the commit uses `attrs = attrs or {}` and only copies when `tag != "legend"`. For legends (`legend_tag()`) the caller's own dict is kept, and the following `attrs["class"] += " " + required_css_class` mutates it in place. The caller's attrs dict is modified and the class accumulates on repeated rendering. Fixed by always copying attrs first.

findings.description: For tag == "legend", `attrs` is no longer copied. Previously `{**attrs, "for": ...}` always produced a fresh dict. Now `attrs = attrs or {}` leaves the caller's dict in place. If the field is required and the form has `required_css_class`, the following `attrs["class"] += ...` or `attrs["class"] = ...` mutates the caller's dict. Reusing one attrs dict across several `legend_tag(attrs=...)` calls, such as a shared dict in a template tag or loop, makes the class list grow with each call (`foo required required ...`). It also leaks `required_css_class` into fields that are not required. This is a regression from the old copy behavior.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty regexes and the same failure mechanism. It states that "`_raw_start_re` needs `\s+` after `{%`" and that the end regexes need "`[^\S\n]+`", so tags like `{%verbatim%}` and `{%endcomment%}` are no longer recognized. As a result, their content is "tokenized as live template syntax" or the tag is "never closed", which matches the known bug.
ground_truth: The new lexer regexes for raw blocks require at least one whitespace character after `{%`: `_raw_start_re` uses `\s+` before comment/verbatim, and the end regexes use `[^\S\n]+` before endcomment/endverbatim. Django accepts tags written without spaces, e.g. `{%comment%}`, `{%verbatim%}` and `{%endverbatim%}`. Those are no longer recognized as raw-block delimiters, so their contents are tokenized and parsed as template code (wrong output or TemplateSyntaxError). Fixed by changing `+` to `*`.

findings.description: The raw-block regexes are stricter than the old tokenization. `_raw_start_re` needs `\s+` after `{%`, and the `comment` and unnamed `verbatim` end regexes need `[^\S\n]+` between `{%` and `endcomment`/`endverbatim`. The old lexer and parser accepted `{%verbatim%}...{%endverbatim%}` and `{%endcomment%}` because they compared the stripped content. Now `{%verbatim%}` is not detected at all, so its content is tokenized as live template syntax. A comment closed with `{%endcomment%}` is never closed, so the rest of the template is swallowed as text and parsing fails with an unclosed tag. This regresses existing templates that omit the spaces.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It points to the `[^\S\n]+` in the end regexes and the `\s+` in `_raw_start_re`, which require whitespace after `{%`. It notes that tags written without spaces, such as `{%endcomment%}` and `{%verbatim%}`, are therefore not recognized as raw delimiters, which breaks parsing. This is the same mechanism and the same consequence as the known bug.
ground_truth: The new lexer regexes for raw blocks require at least one whitespace character after `{%`: `_raw_start_re` uses `\s+` before comment/verbatim, and the end regexes use `[^\S\n]+` before endcomment/endverbatim. Django accepts tags written without spaces, e.g. `{%comment%}`, `{%verbatim%}` and `{%endverbatim%}`. Those are no longer recognized as raw-block delimiters, so their contents are tokenized and parsed as template code (wrong output or TemplateSyntaxError). Fixed by changing `+` to `*`.

findings.description: The new closing-tag regexes for comment and unnamed verbatim blocks require at least one whitespace character after `{%` (`[^\S\n]+`). `_raw_start_re` likewise requires `\s+` after `{%`. Tags written without spaces, such as `{%endcomment%}` or `{%endverbatim%}`, are still valid block tags and are matched by `tag_re`, and the parser accepts them. Once any raw-aware path is taken, for example because another `{% comment %}` appears in the template, the lexer treats `{%endcomment%}` as plain text instead of the closing tag. The parser then never sees the end token and raises 'Unclosed tag' or swallows the rest of the template. Likewise a `{%verbatim%}` opener is not detected as raw. Templates that rendered correctly before are therefore broken. The named-verbatim regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, which is inconsistent with these.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect: "The closing-tag regexes `_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` require at least one non-newline whitespace character between `{%` and `endcomment`/`endverbatim`", so tags like `{%endverbatim%}` are no longer recognized. It also notes that the fast-path selection depends on a whitespace-separated opener, which touches on `_raw_start_re`'s `\s+`. This is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism (`+` where `*` is needed), and it would lead a maintainer to the fix.
ground_truth: The new lexer regexes for raw blocks require at least one whitespace character after `{%`: `_raw_start_re` uses `\s+` before comment/verbatim, and the end regexes use `[^\S\n]+` before endcomment/endverbatim. Django accepts tags written without spaces, e.g. `{%comment%}`, `{%verbatim%}` and `{%endverbatim%}`. Those are no longer recognized as raw-block delimiters, so their contents are tokenized and parsed as template code (wrong output or TemplateSyntaxError). Fixed by changing `+` to `*`.

findings.description: The closing-tag regexes `_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` require at least one non-newline whitespace character between `{%` and `endcomment`/`endverbatim`. The old lexer compared the stripped tag content, so `{%endverbatim%}` and `{%endcomment%}` worked. The opener is still recognized without whitespace, because `_raw_end_tag_re` strips the content. As a result, `{%verbatim%}...{%endverbatim%}` (or `{%comment%}...{%endcomment%}`) in debug mode, or in any template that also has a spaced opener, never finds its closer. The rest of the template is treated as text and the parser raises an unclosed-tag error. Behaviour also depends on the code path: the fast path in `tokenize()` is chosen only when no whitespace-separated opener exists, and `DebugLexer` always uses the raw-aware splitter. Named verbatim closers use `[^\S\n]*`, so they are inconsistent with unnamed ones.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect: "resolves every string in order_by with F(order_by). Strings with a descending prefix ("-id"...), the random ordering "?" ... raises FieldError". This is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug, and it proposes the same fix: strip the '-' prefix and handle '?'.
ground_truth: The new `Query.orderby_issubset_groupby` property resolves every string in `order_by` with `F(order_by)`. Order-by strings may carry a "-" prefix for descending order or be "?" for random order, which are not field names. So e.g. `.values("is_staff").annotate(latest=Max(...)).order_by("-latest").count()` crashes with `FieldError: Cannot resolve keyword '-latest' into field`. Fixed by stripping the "-" prefix and returning False for "?".

findings.description: orderby_issubset_groupby resolves every string in order_by with F(order_by). Strings with a descending prefix ("-id", "-name"), the random ordering "?", and strings with a table-qualified or extra reference are not valid F() names. For a grouped query such as `Book.objects.values('contact__name').annotate(c=Count('id')).order_by('-contact__name').count()`, resolving F('-contact__name') raises FieldError ("Cannot resolve keyword '-contact__name'"). Before this change count() simply cleared the ordering and worked, so this is a crash regression for common order_by usage. The code needs to strip the '-' prefix and handle '?' and similar cases, for example by using the same order-by normalization as the compiler.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says "Descending order_by strings such as "-id" are passed to F(order_by).resolve_expression(q)" and that this "raises FieldError (Cannot resolve keyword '-id')". It also notes that "?" fails the same way. That is the same faulty code, the same failure mechanism, and the same crash on .count() as the known bug.
ground_truth: The new `Query.orderby_issubset_groupby` property resolves every string in `order_by` with `F(order_by)`. Order-by strings may carry a "-" prefix for descending order or be "?" for random order, which are not field names. So e.g. `.values("is_staff").annotate(latest=Max(...)).order_by("-latest").count()` crashes with `FieldError: Cannot resolve keyword '-latest' into field`. Fixed by stripping the "-" prefix and returning False for "?".

findings.description: Descending order_by strings such as "-id" are passed to F(order_by).resolve_expression(q). F does not parse the "-" prefix, so this raises FieldError (Cannot resolve keyword '-id'). "?" for random ordering fails the same way. Calling .count() or .aggregate() on a values().annotate() queryset with an explicit group_by and .order_by('-field') will therefore crash. Before this change, the ordering was cleared without being resolved. Resolved OrderBy expressions also never compare equal to the Col objects in group_by, so descending ordering is never treated as a subset.

justification: Finding 0 pins down the same defect: orderby_issubset_groupby wraps string order_by entries in F(...), and "order_by strings can carry a '-' direction prefix or be '?'". It gives the same failure: F('-id') raises FieldError when .count() is called on values().annotate() querysets.
ground_truth: The new `Query.orderby_issubset_groupby` property resolves every string in `order_by` with `F(order_by)`. Order-by strings may carry a "-" prefix for descending order or be "?" for random order, which are not field names. So e.g. `.values("is_staff").annotate(latest=Max(...)).order_by("-latest").count()` crashes with `FieldError: Cannot resolve keyword '-latest' into field`. Fixed by stripping the "-" prefix and returning False for "?".

findings.description: orderby_issubset_groupby wraps each string order_by entry in F(...).resolve_expression(). order_by strings can carry a '-' direction prefix or be '?', for example order_by('-id') or order_by('?'). F('-id') cannot be resolved to a field, so it raises FieldError (Cannot resolve keyword '-id'). This is reached from get_aggregation() for any query with a tuple group_by (values().annotate()) and a descending string ordering, so .count() or .aggregate() on such querysets now crashes. They worked before this change.

justification: The known bug is that alogin()/alogout() replaced the request.user updates with request.auser updates, which leaves request.user stale. Finding 0 covers alogin: it says the old `request.user = user` block was "replaced by an `auser` override, not extended with one". Finding 1 covers alogout: it says the function "no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser". Both describe the exact defect and the same fix (update both attributes).
ground_truth: To keep `request.auser()` in sync, the commit changes `alogin()` and `alogout()` to replace `request.auser` instead of setting `request.user`. It drops the old `if hasattr(request, "user"): request.user = user` and `request.user = AnonymousUser()` branches. After `await alogin(...)` or `await alogout(...)`, `request.user` still holds the previous user (e.g. still authenticated after logout), so sync code paths and templates see stale authentication state. Fixed by updating both `request.user` and `request.auser` when present.

findings.description: alogin() no longer updates request.user. The old `if hasattr(request, "user"): request.user = user` block was replaced by an `auser` override, not extended with one. After `await alogin(request, user)`, synchronous code that reads `request.user` (templates, context processors, sync middleware or views) still sees the old user, usually AnonymousUser. This regresses existing behavior. Both `user` and `auser` should be updated.

alogout() no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser. After `await alogout(request)`, `request.user` still holds the logged-out user, so later code that reads it treats the request as authenticated. This is a regression and a security concern. Only `request.auser` is replaced. Both attributes should be reset.

justification: Finding 0 states that alogin() "no longer sets request.user" because the old hasattr(request, "user") branch was replaced with an auser-only update, leaving request.user stale. It also proposes updating both attributes, which is the actual fix. Finding 1 describes the same mechanism in alogout(): request.user "still refers to the previously authenticated user". Both are halves of the known bug.
ground_truth: To keep `request.auser()` in sync, the commit changes `alogin()` and `alogout()` to replace `request.auser` instead of setting `request.user`. It drops the old `if hasattr(request, "user"): request.user = user` and `request.user = AnonymousUser()` branches. After `await alogin(...)` or `await alogout(...)`, `request.user` still holds the previous user (e.g. still authenticated after logout), so sync code paths and templates see stale authentication state. Fixed by updating both `request.user` and `request.auser` when present.

findings.description: alogin() no longer sets request.user. The old `if hasattr(request, "user"): request.user = user` block was replaced by one that only updates request.auser. After `await alogin(request, user)`, request.user keeps the old user, usually AnonymousUser. This is a regression for existing async code and for sync code that reads request.user afterwards. It also leaves request.user and request.auser disagreeing. The fix should update both attributes.

alogout() no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser. Only request.auser is replaced. After `await alogout(request)`, request.user still refers to the previously authenticated user. Views, templates and permission checks that read request.user in the rest of the request will still treat the user as logged in. This is a regression and a security-relevant inconsistency with the sync logout().

justification: The known bug is that the change dropped the `request.user` updates, so `request.user` goes stale after `alogin()` and `alogout()`. Finding 0 states this for alogin: "Nothing updates request.user any more... request.user stays the old user". Finding 1 states it for alogout: "alogout() no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser... request.user still holds the logged-out user". Both describe the same defect.
ground_truth: To keep `request.auser()` in sync, the commit changes `alogin()` and `alogout()` to replace `request.auser` instead of setting `request.user`. It drops the old `if hasattr(request, "user"): request.user = user` and `request.user = AnonymousUser()` branches. After `await alogin(...)` or `await alogout(...)`, `request.user` still holds the previous user (e.g. still authenticated after logout), so sync code paths and templates see stale authentication state. Fixed by updating both `request.user` and `request.auser` when present.

findings.description: alogin() used to set request.user, and the patch replaces that with a request.auser override. Nothing updates request.user any more. With AuthenticationMiddleware, request.user stays the old user (or AnonymousUser) after alogin(), so sync code and templates that read request.user see stale data. Any request with only `user` set and no `auser` is not updated at all. Upstream's fix sets both attributes.

alogout() no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser. It only replaces request.auser. After alogout(), request.user still holds the logged-out user, which is a security-relevant regression: later code or templates in the same request still see an authenticated user. Requests that have `user` but no `auser` are also not reset.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect: "If a caller passes `sort_keys` through `serializers.serialize('yaml', ..., sort_keys=...)`, `yaml.dump` receives the keyword twice and raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`." It also proposes the same fix, `self.options.setdefault('sort_keys', False)`.
ground_truth: The commit replaces a custom dict representer with `yaml.dump(..., Dumper=DjangoSafeDumper, sort_keys=False, **self.options)`. If the caller passes `sort_keys` as a serializer option (e.g. `serializers.serialize("yaml", qs, sort_keys=True)`), the keyword is given twice and `yaml.dump()` raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Fixed with `self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)`.

findings.description: `sort_keys=False` is now hard-coded next to `**self.options`. If a caller passes `sort_keys` through `serializers.serialize('yaml', ..., sort_keys=...)`, `yaml.dump` receives the keyword twice and raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Previously the option was accepted, because the dict representer ignored it. Using `self.options.setdefault('sort_keys', False)` would avoid the crash.

justification: Finding [0] describes the same defect as the known bug. It says that passing `sort_keys` as a serializer option makes `yaml.dump` receive the keyword twice and raise "TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'". It also proposes the same fix, `setdefault`.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It points out that `force_str(password)` in PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode decodes bytes as UTF-8, so a bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 "now raises UnicodeDecodeError". It also notes the decode step is unnecessary because pbkdf2 accepts bytes, which is the fix. It does not mention MD5, but the PBKDF2 mechanism and fix are the same as in the known bug.
ground_truth: To accept both str and bytes, the commit adds `password = force_str(password)` (and the same for salt) in `PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode()` and `MD5PasswordHasher.encode()`. `force_str` decodes bytes as UTF-8, so a bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 (a perfectly valid password value) now raises `UnicodeDecodeError` instead of being hashed. Fixed by passing the password through unchanged in PBKDF2 (`pbkdf2()` accepts bytes) and hashing `force_bytes(salt) + force_bytes(password)` in MD5.

findings.description: PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode now runs force_str(password), which decodes bytes as UTF-8. Before this change, pbkdf2() accepted arbitrary bytes passwords through force_bytes. A bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 now raises UnicodeDecodeError, which is a regression for callers that passed raw bytes. The password only needs to be converted to bytes for hashing, so the decode step is unnecessary. The salt does need to be str, because it is embedded in the encoded string.

justification: Finding 0 points at the `force_str(password)` call in PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode(). It says a bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 now raises UnicodeDecodeError, and it proposes keeping the password as bytes. This is the same mechanism as the known bug and matches its fix. The finding does not mention MD5, but the defect it describes is the same.
ground_truth: To accept both str and bytes, the commit adds `password = force_str(password)` (and the same for salt) in `PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode()` and `MD5PasswordHasher.encode()`. `force_str` decodes bytes as UTF-8, so a bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 (a perfectly valid password value) now raises `UnicodeDecodeError` instead of being hashed. Fixed by passing the password through unchanged in PBKDF2 (`pbkdf2()` accepts bytes) and hashing `force_bytes(salt) + force_bytes(password)` in MD5.

findings.description: PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode() now calls force_str(password) before pbkdf2(). A bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 now raises UnicodeDecodeError, for example make_password(b'\xff\xfe') or check_password(b'\xff', encoded). Before this change, pbkdf2() applied force_bytes() to the password and hashed the raw bytes without trouble. This regresses the default hasher, since it needlessly round-trips bytes through str. The password should stay as bytes, or be converted with force_bytes() only.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect as the known bug. It quotes that `hostname_re` "matches a single DNS label only" and that the pattern "omits `DomainNameValidator.domain_re`". As a result, bare multi-label domains like `docs.djangoproject.com` no longer match and are not linked. It also proposes the same fix as the known bug: appending `domain_re` after `hostname_re`.
ground_truth: In `urlize`, the simple-URL regex for bare domains is changed to use `DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` before the TLD. `hostname_re` matches a single DNS label (no dots), so bare multi-label domains without `www.` or a scheme, e.g. `docs.djangoproject.com`, no longer match and are not turned into links (`djangoproject.com` still works). Fixed by appending `DomainNameValidator.domain_re`, which matches the additional dotted labels.

findings.description: `DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` matches a single DNS label only. The new `simple_url_2_re` omits `DomainNameValidator.domain_re`, which covers the additional dotted labels. As a result, bare multi-label domains such as `sub.example.com`, `docs.djangoproject.com/path` and `mail.example.net` no longer match. The old pattern `\w[^@]+\.(com|...)` accepted them, so `urlize` stops linking them. This is a regression for existing users. The pattern should be `hostname_re` followed by `(?:domain_re)` and then the TLD.

ground_truth: In `urlize`, the simple-URL regex for bare domains is changed to use `DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` before the TLD. `hostname_re` matches a single DNS label (no dots), so bare multi-label domains without `www.` or a scheme, e.g. `docs.djangoproject.com`, no longer match and are not turned into links (`djangoproject.com` still works). Fixed by appending `DomainNameValidator.domain_re`, which matches the additional dotted labels.

findings.description: `DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` matches only a single DNS label with no dots. `domain_re`, which matches the further `.label` parts, is not included. The new `simple_url_2_re` therefore only matches `label.tld`, such as `example.com`. Bare multi-label hosts like `sub.example.com`, `mail.example.co.com` or `foo.bar.org/path` (no scheme, no `www.`) no longer match, so `urlize` stops linking them. This regresses previously working behavior. The pattern needs `(?:{DomainNameValidator.domain_re})` between the hostname part and the TLD.

findings.description: `DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` matches a single DNS label with no dots. The new `simple_url_2_re` is `^(?!http)<one label>\.(com|edu|...)($|/.*)$`, so it only accepts `label.tld`. Words with subdomains and no `www.` or scheme, such as `docs.djangoproject.com`, `mail.google.com` or `foo.example.org/path`, used to be urlized and now are left as plain text. `DomainNameValidator.domain_re` (the repeated `.label` part) needs to be included between the hostname and the TLD.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the bug exactly. It notes that the new wrapper is "always a plain synchronous function", so for `async def` views "iscoroutinefunction returns False" and the decorated async views break. It also says an async variant of the wrapper is needed, which matches both the known bug and its fix.
ground_truth: To avoid mutating the original view, `non_atomic_requests()` now wraps the view in a new synchronous `def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return view(*args, **kwargs)`. For an async view this wrapper is a sync function returning a coroutine, so Django no longer recognizes the decorated view as async (`iscoroutinefunction` is False), and async views decorated with `@transaction.non_atomic_requests` break. Fixed by creating an `async def` wrapper when the view is a coroutine function.

findings.description: The new wrapper is always a plain synchronous function. When `non_atomic_requests` is applied to an `async def` view, the result is no longer a coroutine function, so `iscoroutinefunction` returns False. Django's handler will then treat the view as sync and run it in a thread, and it will get back an un-awaited coroutine instead of an HttpResponse. Async views decorated with `@non_atomic_requests` therefore break with an error like 'didn't return an HttpResponse object. It returned an unawaited coroutine'. This is a regression for existing users, and the wrapper needs an async variant.

It also proposes an async wrapper as the fix. This is the same mechanism and the same remedy as the known bug.
ground_truth: To avoid mutating the original view, `non_atomic_requests()` now wraps the view in a new synchronous `def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return view(*args, **kwargs)`. For an async view this wrapper is a sync function returning a coroutine, so Django no longer recognizes the decorated view as async (`iscoroutinefunction` is False), and async views decorated with `@transaction.non_atomic_requests` break. Fixed by creating an `async def` wrapper when the view is a coroutine function.

findings.description: The new wrapper is always a plain synchronous function. When `non_atomic_requests` is applied to an `async def` view, `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction(wrapper)` returns False. Django then treats the view as sync. Under ASGI it is run through `sync_to_async`, and under WSGI it is called directly. Either way the view returns an unawaited coroutine, which gives "didn't return an HttpResponse ... returned an unawaited coroutine" errors. This is a regression for existing async views decorated with `@non_atomic_requests`, which previously worked because the original function was returned. The fix needs an async wrapper for coroutine functions.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect as the known bug. It says "The new wrapper is always a plain synchronous `def`" and that when applied to an async view "the result is no longer a coroutine function", which breaks Django's `iscoroutinefunction` check. Its proposed fix, an async def wrapper, is the same as the actual fix.
ground_truth: To avoid mutating the original view, `non_atomic_requests()` now wraps the view in a new synchronous `def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return view(*args, **kwargs)`. For an async view this wrapper is a sync function returning a coroutine, so Django no longer recognizes the decorated view as async (`iscoroutinefunction` is False), and async views decorated with `@transaction.non_atomic_requests` break. Fixed by creating an `async def` wrapper when the view is a coroutine function.

findings.description: The new wrapper is always a plain synchronous `def`. When `non_atomic_requests` is applied to an `async def` view, the result is no longer a coroutine function. It is a sync function that returns an unawaited coroutine. Django's handlers use `iscoroutinefunction(view)` to decide how to adapt the view. Under ASGI the view would be run in a thread and return a coroutine object, which raises 'didn't return an HttpResponse object... unawaited coroutine'. Under WSGI, `async_to_sync` would not be applied. Async views decorated with `@non_atomic_requests` therefore break, which is a regression. The wrapper needs to be an `async def` (or be marked as a coroutine function) when `view` is async.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says `path.startswith(self._route)` / `removeprefix` are given a lazy translation proxy, which causes a TypeError or failure to match. It also proposes the same fix, `str(self._route)`, which is the known bug and its fix.
ground_truth: To skip the regex for converter-less routes, `RoutePattern.match()` now compares the path with `self._route` using string operations (`==`, `startswith`, `removeprefix`). `_route` can be a lazy translation object (`gettext_lazy()` routes, e.g. with i18n URL patterns). Lazy proxies don't behave like `str` for `str.startswith()` / `str.removeprefix()`, so such routes fail to match or raise. Fixed by coercing the route with `str(self._route)` at match time.

findings.description: In the new non-endpoint, no-converter branch, `path.startswith(self._route)` and `path.removeprefix(self._route)` use `self._route` directly. For translated routes (`path(_('translated/'), include(...))`) it is a lazy string proxy, not a `str`. `str.startswith` raises `TypeError` for it, so resolving any include-style prefix with a lazily translated route crashes. The old regex path handled this through `LocaleRegexDescriptor`, which evaluates the translation for the active language. The new code should use `str(self._route)`. Matching also ignores the active language, because `converters` is computed once.

That is the same mechanism and the same fix as the known bug.

Lazy proxies don't behave like `str` for `str.startswith()` / `str.removeprefix()`, so such routes fail to match or raise. Fixed by coercing the route with `str(self._route)` at match time.

findings.description: For non-endpoint routes without converters, `path.startswith(self._route)` and `path.removeprefix(self._route)` use `self._route` directly. For translated routes (`gettext_lazy`) this is a lazy proxy, not a `str`, so both calls raise `TypeError`. The old code went through `self.regex`, which resolved the translation via `LocaleRegexDescriptor`. This also ignores the active language, because it never uses the translated value. It would break `include()` or prefix patterns with lazy-translated routes such as `path(_('translated/'), include(...))`. Wrapping the route in `str()` would avoid the crash.

findings.description: The new converter-less branches use self._route directly, but for translated routes (path(_('translated/'), ...)) it is a lazy proxy, not a str. `path.startswith(self._route)` and `path.removeprefix(self._route)` raise TypeError for a lazy proxy, so non-endpoint patterns such as translated include() prefixes would crash on resolve. The old regex path avoided this by using str(route) and the language-specific regex. The endpoint `==` comparison and the prefix check also don't explicitly evaluate the lazy string for the active language. The fix is to use str(self._route) at match time.
